papers.title: Do Machine Learning-Guided Proactive Full Capacity Protocols Mitigate Emergency Department Overcrowding? A Simulation-Based Evaluation
papers.abstract: Objective: Emergency department (ED) overcrowding threatens care quality, yet Full Capacity Protocols (FCPs) are typically activated only after crowding thresholds have been exceeded. This study evaluated whether machine learning-guided proactive FCP activation improves ED crowding control compared with conventional reactive activation. Materials and Methods: We developed and validated an integrated machine learning and discrete-event simulation framework representing ED patient flow and capacity management. An embedded machine learning model predicted hourly waiting-room crowding six hours ahead and triggered proactive FCP activation. Using empirically calibrated operational parameters from a large US hospital, we compared proactive and reactive deployment strategies over a 365-day simulation horizon with 10 independent replications. Outcomes included ED length of stay, wait time, percentage of time above the crowding threshold, number of FCP activations, and protocol duration. Results: Proactive deployment produced statistically significant reductions in the percentage of time above the crowding threshold and average protocol duration across all threshold settings. It also reduced crowding variability and extreme congestion events, resulting in smoother ED operations. Although proactive deployment generally improved ED length of stay and wait time, these differences were not statistically significant. Conclusion: Embedding machine learning predictions within an operational simulation enables proactive, prediction-guided capacity management before severe congestion develops. These findings support the feasibility and potential value of proactive FCP deployment as a decision-support strategy for improving ED crowding control and provide evidence to support prospective implementation in clinical practice.

papers.title: LLM2Cert: LLM Synthesis of Certificates with SMT/Lean Verification
papers.abstract: Lyapunov functions and barrier certificates give state-space guarantees of stability and safety, but synthesizing and verifying them---especially for nonlinear, high-dimensional systems---remains an open challenge. Existing pipelines verify candidates with numerical solvers (sum-of-squares programs), interval methods, or satisfiability-modulo-theories (SMT) solvers, which often require relaxations, are conservative, or scale poorly with model dimension and nonlinearity. These limitations have also shaped benchmark design: standard test suites are dominated by low-dimensional polynomial systems chosen to suit what solvers can handle rather than what engineering applications require. We address both sides of this challenge. First, we introduce DynaCertBench, a benchmark of 105 instances: 80 non-redundant systems curated from the literature, extended with high-dimensional and control-constrained variants and new nonlinearly coupled systems, comprehensively spanning stability, region-of-attraction, forward-invariance, and safety tasks. Second, we present LLM2Cert, an LLM-driven framework that synthesizes candidate certificates and verifies them against their proof obligations: each obligation is routed to an SMT solver or directly to the Lean Proof-Repair agent. On DynaCertBench, LLM2Cert verifies 81 of 105 instances ($77.1\%$), a $17.1$ percentage point improvement over one-shot proposal without feedback. On the 81 fixed certificates, LLM2Cert verifies 22 that All-SMT leaves unresolved. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/llm2cert.

papers.title: Dissipation Bounds and Hardness in Globally Asymptotically Stable Quadratic Systems
papers.abstract: Approximating the maximum retained energy fraction in globally asymptotically stable quadratic systems of growing dimension is NP-hard at every fixed positive additive error below $1/2$, even when strict quartic Lyapunov functions and strictness proofs are constructed in polynomial time and included in the input. Polynomial-factor approximation is also NP-hard for the least dissipated fraction, energy-halving time and structured coefficient distance to loss of asymptotic stability. For a partially damped family, minimum unit-sphere coupling norm equals that distance, with two-sided inverse-square halving-time bounds at distances in $(0,1/2]$ and explicit coefficient factors. Additive hardness persists under structured coefficient perturbations and direct damping, even with global exponential stability, a strict quadratic Lyapunov function and a Hurwitz Jacobian.

papers.title: A Tutte-Like Theorem for Injective Flows on Meshes
papers.abstract: This work proves a theorem regarding injectivity of continuous flows that are defined via discrete vector fields on triangle meshes. In similar fashion to Tutte's embedding, the theorem shows a connection between harmonicity and injectivity. Specifically, a discrete harmonic function is computed over a spherical mesh, and its $90^\circ$-rotated gradients are taken as the vector field. We show that this leads to an injective flow over the mesh, i.e., when two points are advected along the vector field, their trajectories are guaranteed to not intersect. The core insight behind this theorem is that the characterization of the Poincar\'e-Hopf indices of discrete harmonic 1-forms is paralleled in the combinatorial rules for injective vector fields. Similarly to Tutte's embedding, the injective vector field can be computed by simply solving a sparse linear system. Furthermore, it is differentiably dependent on the entries of the Laplacian, enabling unconstrained gradient-based optimization of the vector field while preserving injectivity. The advection itself can be computed by a quick and accurate algorithm. We experimentally validate the injectivity of the results, as well as show examples of differentiable optimization, such as computing an injective approximation to a given non-injective vector field, and fitting an injective vector field to satisfy constraints.

papers.title: Assortment optimization under the perception-adjusted Luce model
papers.abstract: The Perception-Adjusted Luce Model (PALM) introduced by by Echenique et al. (2018) is a sequential choice model that can accommodate violations of regularity and choice overload, behaviors not captured by the utility-maximization framework. Flores et al. (2019) studied the assortment problem under the PALM and proved that, for the case of two levels, there is always an optimal solution that is revenue-ordered by level. They also conjectured that revenue-ordered by levels remain optimal for the general PALM with any number of levels. We resolve this question in the affirmative by showing that every PALM instance admits an optimal assortment that includes, within each level, all products at or above a level-specific revenue threshold. The proof involves first showing how the conjecture which deals with a discrete optimization problem, can be reduced to proving certain property of a related continuous optimization problem. Specifically, we study a continuous refinement of the assortment decision under the same PALM choice rule. Although the refinement permits partial utility selections, we prove it always has an optimum that selects complete revenue tiers. This allows us to show that the assortment problem is polynomial-time solvable when the number of levels is fixed.

papers.title: A Resource Allocation Tournament
papers.abstract: We introduce and analyze a round-robin simultaneous resource allocation contest, motivated by sports leagues and other competitive environments where agents must distribute limited resources across multiple encounters. Players allocate resources in advance to matches against all opponents, and match outcomes are determined by relative allocations. We study two payoff schemes: total points, where players accumulate rewards for each win, and winner-takes-all, where only the tournament winner is rewarded. For three players, we provide complete equilibrium characterizations under both schemes. For four or more players, we show that the total points payoff admits Blotto-type equilibria, while the winner-takes-all payoff requires numerical and algorithmic analysis. To address this, we develop a best-response dynamics algorithm with stochastic inertia and use it to approximate equilibria in games with four and five players.

papers.title: Deep ReLU Networks Can Fail the Best Approximation Property for Continuous Target Functions
papers.abstract: We construct a continuous function on $[-1,1]^2$ for which the infimum of the $L^2$-approximation error over the class of ReLU networks with two hidden layers and architecture $(2,2,1,1)$ is not attained. This counterexample shows that deep ReLU networks do not satisfy the best approximation property in general, even for continuous target functions. Our findings contrast with existing results for shallow neural networks, where ReLU is one of the few activation functions that guarantee the existence of global minima in typical regression tasks. The proof is based on the fact that the breaklines for neurons in the second hidden layer can bend, which breaks the symmetry arguments used in the one-hidden-layer case.

papers.title: Consensus-Aware Co-design of Wireless Multi-Agent Control and Communication Systems
papers.abstract: Autonomous multi-agent control systems (MACSs) enable distributed coordination in emerging applications such as smart power grids and autonomous vehicle or drone networks. In many of these applications, inter-agent communication relies on wireless networks. However, conventional MACS designs neglect the interaction between the communication and control subsystems. At the same time, conventional wireless designs reserve communication resources based on worst-case MACS requirements. Consequently, control performance is degraded and wireless resources are utilized inefficiently. To address these challenges, we propose a consensus-aware co-design approach for MACSs and wireless communication systems. We introduce a system model in which agents achieve consensus by exchanging information through device-to-device (D2D) links that share spectrum with cellular users under limited bandwidth resources. Based on this model, we formulate a joint optimization problem for consensus-topology selection and wireless resource allocation to minimize bandwidth consumption while guaranteeing consensus and satisfying the quality-of-service (QoS) requirements of both MACSs and cellular users. Although the resulting problem is a mixed-integer nonlinear program (NP-hard in general), a structural property of the optimal solution enables a sequential two-stage optimization algorithm with polynomial complexity. Simulations on a smart power grid case study demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves 24-27% bandwidth savings compared with the two baselines while maintaining consensus and satisfying all QoS requirements of the control agents and the communication users.

papers.title: A Transformer-based Approach for Real-time Multi-agent Path Planning with Varying Initial/Final Conditions
papers.abstract: We address the problem of real-time multi-agent path planning under prescribed initial and final configurations, formulated as a high-dimensional optimal control problem subject to inter-agent collision avoidance and obstacle constraints. Classical solvers based on the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or Pontryagin's maximum principle (PMP) become computationally intractable as the number of agents grows, due to the curse of dimensionality and the non-convexity introduced by interaction constraints. We propose OCFormer, a transformer-based neural network that parameterizes the inverse of a coordinate transformation mapping a simple, analytically tractable latent space, in which agents evolve independently under a decoupled Hamiltonian, to the physical space of the coupled, interacting system. The model is trained by minimizing a physics-informed loss comprising the Hamiltonian ODE residual from the PMP and a boundary matching term, without requiring pre-computed trajectory data. The self-attention mechanism endows OCFormer with permutation equivariance over agents, a structural symmetry that prior symplectic network approaches do not natively enforce. When trained on a distribution of boundary conditions, the amortized OCFormer produces near-optimal trajectories for unseen initial and final configurations in a single forward pass ($\sim$220ms), enabling real-time inference without retraining. We further introduce a lightweight transfer learning framework that adapts a pretrained OCFormer to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds via L-BFGS fine-tuning. Numerical experiments on two- and three-dimensional multi-agent navigation with up to 128 agents demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of the proposed approach.

papers.title: Strong Duality Thresholds and Minimum Curvature for the Nearest Rectangular Symplectic Matrix Problem
papers.abstract: We study the nearest rectangular symplectic matrix problem in the squared Frobenius norm for arbitrary targets $T\in\mathbb R^{2n\times2k}$, with $n\ge k$. We prove that its semidefinite relaxation is exact for every target if and only if $n\ge2k-1$. Under this condition, the primal problem, the relaxation, and both Lagrangian dual problems attain the same optimal value. In this range, we derive the exact minimum Rayleigh quotient of the Riemannian Hessian at every feasible point under the Euclidean induced metric, and prove that all second-order stationary points are global minimizers. We also obtain global objective error bounds. We extend the strong-duality and minimum-curvature results to Hermitian positive definite row weights, proving that strong duality holds for every target if and only if the lowest eigenvalue of the weight has complex multiplicity at least $2k-1$. The dual formulation leads to a method whose main iterations use matrices of order $2k$, with $O(k^2)$ iterative storage apart from the full input and output. Across six tested sizes, mean-time speedups are $2.55$--$12.60$ over a Riemannian first-order method and $4.61$--$43.93$ over Jensen--Zimmermann R--TR2; batching gives a further factor of $3.45$--$23.53$ over sequential calls. The theoretical results complete the critical dimensions not covered by Gram convexification and quadratic matrix programming.

papers.title: Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona)
papers.abstract: We propose a new regression method named Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) that directly uses samples to estimate the state and its derivatives at a query point, along with their admissible bounds, without long global training. By casting the values and derivatives at the query and neighbouring samples as latent variables in a constrained optimisation problem, the burden of long training loops becomes one of on-demand local solves. We establish Diona's theoretical properties including finite-sample coverage and, in the noiseless case, convergence to the true state and derivatives under dense sampling. In a nonlinear regression benchmark on six functions of three to eight dimensions, Diona was more accurate than a Gaussian process (GP) on noiseless data especially with denser data sets. Furthermore, as with GP, it produced uncertainty bounds that contained the true value at more than 95% of query points in four functions. Diona's time to a first prediction after a data set update was three to four orders of magnitude shorter than that of the GP, and two to three orders shorter than that of a neural network, which was more accurate but offers no uncertainty quantification. This low latency is paid for by on-demand predictions, so this latency advantage applies when relatively few predictions are needed between data updates.

papers.title: Dispersive Tree Agreements for Multi-Robot Coordination
papers.abstract: Multi-robot coordination of nonlinear systems is naturally formulated as joint-space optimal control subject to constraints over groups of robots. Existing methods that approach joint optimality remain largely centralized, offline, and confined to collision-free motion planning, while decentralized, real-time counterparts target safe navigation without pursuing the joint optimum. This paper develops a decentralized, real-time planner that approaches the joint optimum as an anytime process. We extend a recent single-robot framework that searches dispersive trees of forward-propagated commands for differentially flat systems to coordinate a multi-robot team near-optimally. We first show that the inter-robot coupling can be effectively replaced by some local constraints, under which locally grown dispersive trees contain a near-optimal agreement. It is this structure that the robots pursue by decentralized column generation, negotiating rents on the shared space that guide the search of each robot's tree. The negotiation settles on an agreement whose near-optimality is certified at quiescence. Our protocol, WarpWeaver, implements this negotiation as an asynchronous real-time loop over a receding horizon, and demonstrates effective closure to quiesced agreements even when real-time deadlines cut the negotiation short. In simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time by up to 22% against centralized offline planners on the Dynobench suite and by up to 37% against a decentralized real-time baseline, and nearly doubles the success rate of a task-specific planner on graph connectivity. Hardware experiments on six robots planning onboard demonstrate real-world implementability.

papers.title: On the Gradient Domination of the LQG Problem
papers.abstract: We consider solutions to the linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) regulator problem via policy gradient (PG) methods. Although PG methods have demonstrated strong theoretical guarantees in solving the linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem, despite its nonconvex landscape, their theoretical understanding in the LQG setting remains limited. Notably, the LQG problem lacks gradient dominance in the classical parameterization, i.e., with a dynamic controller, which hinders global convergence guarantees. In this work, we study a PG method for the LQG problem by adopting an alternative parameterization of the set of stabilizing controllers and employing a lifting argument. We refer to this parameterization as a history representation of the control input as it is parameterized by past input and output data from the previous p time-steps. Under this parameterization, the infinite-history LQG optimization reduces to an equivalent static state-feedback LQR problem, allowing us to recover gradient dominance and smoothness. For finite history length p, we establish model-based and model-free convergence guarantees up to a geometrically decaying history-truncation error.

papers.title: Bayesian Ambiguity Contraction-based Adaptive Robust Markov Decision Processes for Adversarial Surveillance Missions
papers.abstract: Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCAs) are envisioned to enable autonomous Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) missions in contested environments, where adversaries may act strategically to deceive or evade detection. These missions pose challenges due to model uncertainty and the need for safe, real-time decision-making. Robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) provide worst-case guarantees but are limited by static ambiguity sets that capture initial uncertainty without adapting to new observations. This paper presents an adaptive RMDP framework tailored to ISR missions with CCAs. We introduce a mission-specific formulation in which the CCA alternates between movement and sensing states. Adversarial uncertainty is represented by finite threat prototypes defining observation, exposure, and state-action transition models. Our approach incrementally refines policies by eliminating inconsistent threat models, allowing the CCA to move from worst-case protection toward more efficient mission policies while maintaining robustness. We establish fixed point stability, agreement with nominal planning as credible sets identify the true node-specific threat prototypes, and a conservative expected value guarantee while those prototypes remain credible. Experiments under Gaussian and non-Gaussian threat models across diverse network topologies show higher mission rewards and fewer exposure events compared to nominal and static robust planners.

papers.title: High-dimensional learning dynamics of multi-pass Stochastic Gradient Descent in multi-index models
papers.abstract: The learning dynamics of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) are believed to play an important role in influencing the generalization properties of trained models. While the precise dynamics of how online (one-pass) SGD optimizes the population risk are now understood in a broad range of high-dimensional problems, a comparable understanding of multi-pass SGD for empirical risk minimization is still largely lacking. In this work, we develop an asymptotically exact characterization of the dynamics of multi-pass SGD for a non-convex multi-index model, in the high-dimensional regime where sample size $n$ and data dimension $d$ increase proportionally. We consider any sub-linear batch size $\kappa \asymp n^\alpha$ with $\alpha \in [0,1)$ and a commensurate ``critical'' scaling of the learning rate, and show that the coordinate-wise dynamics of SGD admit a novel continuous-time scaling limit, given by a system of dynamical mean-field equations that are driven by a scalar Poisson jump process representing the asymptotic limit of SGD sampling noise. This scaling limit connects several previously disparate theories around SGD, namely (i) the classical interpretation of SGD as an approximation to gradient flow on the empirical risk, (ii) the characterization of online SGD via an autonomous ODE in its overlap statistics, and (iii) the coincidence between multi-pass SGD dynamics and diffusion approximations in least-squares problems. We illustrate how these perspectives are recovered by specializing our result to small learning rates, large sample sizes, and linear models, respectively. Outside of these specializations, the scaling limit of SGD is distinct both from diffusion approximations and gradient flow, and may enable SGD to converge to local optima of the non-convex empirical risk with different statistical properties.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning and Operational Research: A Review of Methodological Integration and Research Directions
papers.abstract: The growing demand for real-time, data-driven decision-making in complex and dynamic systems is placing increasing pressure on Operational Research (OR) methodologies. Sequential decision-making under uncertainty has long been studied in OR through Markov decision processes, dynamic programming, and their approximations, and reinforcement learning (RL) provides simulation-based methods for learning decision policies in such problems. Recent research shows an increasing interest in integrating RL with OR to address dynamic decision-making problems and enhance heuristic and exact methods for combinatorial optimization. The overarching goal across these efforts is to improve solution quality, computational efficiency, and robustness. Given the diversity of integration approaches and application settings, there is a clear need for a systematic and technically detailed review of how RL empowers OR methods. To address this gap, this paper presents a structured review of two methodological roles of RL in OR. The first concerns sequential decision problems in dynamic environments, where states evolve and decisions are repeated over time. The second concerns static combinatorial optimization problems, where inputs are fixed before the solution process begins and RL either constructs solutions or supports heuristic and exact algorithms. Digital twins provide an optional deployment and evaluation layer for training, testing, and validating these methods. We critically synthesize recent advances across these roles and uses, highlighting their advantages, implementation requirements, limitations, and challenges. Finally, we consolidate guidance on when the reviewed approaches may be considered and outline directions for future research on the methodological and practical integration of RL and OR.

papers.title: Dynamic Active Fleet Sizing of Heterogeneous UAV Relays for Post-Disaster Communication Networks
papers.abstract: Uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) communication systems are increasingly used to provide temporary connectivity when ground communication infrastructure is damaged by disasters such as hurricanes and wildfires. However, the amount of aerial support required changes as ground networks recover and communication demand evolves. We focus on dynamically adjusting the number and allocation of actively deployed UAVs within a fixed available fleet. We develop a model predictive control (MPC) framework for dynamic fleet sizing of heterogeneous UAV relays during post-disaster communication recovery. The framework accounts for communication demand, ground network recovery, heterogeneous UAV operation, UAV energy availability, and backhaul capacity, which limits how much relayed traffic can be transmitted to the external communication network. The resulting formulation is a convex quadratic program that supports efficient online fleet sizing and deployment decisions. We evaluate the framework using seven historical disaster recovery case studies based on Federal Communications Commission reports, together with four backhaul scenarios and sensitivity analyses. Results show that required active UAV fleet size varies considerably throughout recovery, while backhaul capacity and fleet composition affect communication performance, highlighting the value of adapting active fleet size over time.

papers.title: Model Predictive Control of Wind Turbines: A Model-Oriented Review of Prediction Models, Control Objectives, and Nonlinear Aerodynamic Formulations
papers.abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) has been applied to wind-turbine regulation with markedly different internal prediction models, ranging from linearized low-order turbine models to nonlinear, aeroelastic, floating, and data-driven predictors. This review organizes the literature primarily by the model propagated by the controller and treats model order, predictor representation, MPC formulation, control objective, and validation plant as separate descriptors. Primary studies show that low-order linear or piecewise-affine predictors are attractive for constrained power and speed regulation, whereas flexible drivetrain, structural, and floating models are needed when drivetrain twist, tower motion, blade loads, or platform dynamics are explicit control quantities. Nonlinear and economic MPC studies further demonstrate coordinated pitch/torque control across broad operating regions, while preview, repetitive, and data-driven formulations address wind prediction, periodic loads, and model mismatch. Particular attention is given to aerodynamic pitch dependence: variable-pitch turbine dynamics can be non-affine with respect to applied pitch, and the term NMPC alone does not prove that the original nonlinear pitch map is retained inside the optimizer. The review therefore adopts a conservative, equation-based classification for direct nonlinear applied-pitch propagation. Here, direct nonlinear applied-pitch propagation means that the applied pitch at each prediction step is evaluated inside the original nonlinear aerodynamic map, rather than replacing that dependence by a linearized, scheduled, piecewise-affine, or learned surrogate. The literature supports a remaining integration challenge at the intersection of flexible drivetrain prediction, nonlinear aerodynamic pitch treatment, explicit constraints and load objectives, and validated adaptive or learned model correction.

papers.title: Exact controllability and rapid stabilization of linear difference delay equations and one-dimensional hyperbolic systems
papers.abstract: This paper addresses exact controllability and rapid stabilization issues for linear difference delay systems with finitely many pointwise delays. We first establish a criterion for exact controllability in $L^r$, $r \in [1, +\infty)$, characterized by a necessary and sufficient Hautus-type frequency-domain condition. The sufficiency of this condition in $L^r$ was already known [https://hal.science/hal-04830757/], whereas its necessity had previously been established only in $L^1$ [arXiv:2210.13590]. We answer [arXiv:2210.13590, Conjecture 3.8] by proving that this condition is also necessary for $r \in (1, +\infty)$. The analysis is based on rewriting the system as an evolution equation in a suitable Banach space, which allows one to apply duality arguments in the spirit of [https://doi.org/10.1137/S036301299119795X]. Building on this controllability analysis and the abstract stabilization framework developed in [https://doi.org/10.1137/S0363012996301609, arXiv:1301.5744], we prove that our exact controllability criterion in $L^r$ is also a sufficient condition for rapid stabilization in $L^2$, i.e., that the system of interest can be stabilized by a family of state feedback control laws ensuring that the closed-loop system is exponentially stable in $L^2$ with an arbitrarily large decay rate. As an application, we extend our results to linear one-dimensional hyperbolic partial differential equations, which can be reduced to linear difference delay systems via the method of characteristics, obtaining also a necessary and sufficient frequency-domain criterion for exact controllability in $L^r$, $r\in [1, +\infty)$, which, as before, is a sufficient condition for rapid stabilization in $L^2$.

papers.title: Strongly Regular Graph Construction via Quadratic Binary Optimization
papers.abstract: Strongly regular graphs, hereafter SRGs, are highly structured combinatorial objects of central interest in algebraic graph theory and quantum information, whose explicit construction becomes rapidly intractable as the number of vertices grows; Conway's still unresolved $99$-graph problem is an emblematic example. The matrix equation defining SRGs is quadratic in the binary edge variables, so the natural penalty enforcing it, a sum of squared residuals, is quartic and lies outside quadratic unconstrained binary optimization, known as QUBO. We prove a considerably stronger obstruction, namely that no quadratic function of the edge variables has the labeled SRGs as its exact set of global minimizers, except for three degenerate families given by the perfect matchings, the cocktail-party graphs and the pentagon. In particular, we formally establish that the $99$-vertex graph of Conway's problem cannot be obtained from any QUBO over the edge variables without auxiliary variables. Guided by this theorem we develop two complementary algorithms. The first operates within pure QUBO, solves the degenerate families exactly, and beyond them works as a generate--prune--verify pipeline whose output is a reduced set of candidates certified by a polynomial-time classical test. The second solves the full problem by quadratizing this quartic penalty through Rosenberg auxiliary variables, whose number grows as $\Theta(N^3)$ with the number of vertices $N$. We test the pure-QUBO route under simulated annealing on all feasible families with at most $18$ vertices and the auxiliary-variable route on representative targets up to $16$ vertices, and tabulate the algebraically feasible parameter sets for graphs with at most $49$ vertices.

papers.title: Continuous-time analysis and algorithms for linear and convex quadratic programs via exactly solvable differential inclusions
papers.abstract: Linear and convex quadratic programs are fundamental problems in optimization. While many methods have been developed for solving these programs in large-scale applications, to our knowledge none have attempted to solve their continuous-time gradient flow, a differential inclusion, in full generality without assumptions beyond feasibility. Recent work solved the gradient flows in two special cases, basis pursuit and the lasso, and obtained competitive algorithms. Motivated by these results, we solve the general case exactly. Using the minimal selection principle for monotone differential inclusions, we show that the trajectory of the gradient flow consists of finitely many pieces, each obtained from one nonnegative least-squares problem. Its final piece yields an optimal solution or a certificate of unboundedness. This analysis leads to two algorithms. The first algorithm is exact, terminates after finitely many steps, and applies to linear programs and projections onto polyhedra. The second algorithm, which we call minimal selection descent, discretizes the gradient flow for general convex quadratic programs. Its iterates converge to an optimal solution when one exists and otherwise certify unboundedness. We apply both algorithms to a positivity-preserving limiter for a discontinuous Galerkin scheme and to optimal control problems for the Poisson and heat equations. In the limiter, the first algorithm conserves the total mass more accurately than the state-of-the-art Douglas--Rachford splitting method. On the control problems, minimal selection descent reaches the optimal value to machine precision and is competitive in time with commercial and open-source solvers.

papers.title: Safety-constrained position tracking of a flexible transmission system
papers.abstract: We consider safety-constrained position tracking for a flexible transmission system consisting of a torsional shaft driven by a motor and connected to a gravitationally loaded inertia. The coupled PDE-ODE dynamics admit a semilinear formulation in which the linear input-output system is impedance passive and the gravitational torque enters as a bounded, globally Lipschitz perturbation. We establish an energy dissipation inequality for the nonlinear model and show that a position-funnel controller with supervised damping admits a unique global closed-loop trajectory. In particular, the motor-angle tracking error remains strictly inside a prescribed time-varying funnel, which can be chosen to enforce safety bounds on the motor angle.

papers.title: Control, stability, and stabilization of some classes of linear time-delay systems
papers.abstract: This monograph presents a selection of the author's recent works on the control, stability, and stabilization of some classes of linear time-delay systems. After a detailed introduction to topics related to time-delay systems covered in the monograph, its main contents are presented in a series of mostly independent chapters.

papers.title: Scaling Local Solvers with the Many-Body Expansion
papers.abstract: We introduce a Many-Body Expansion framework for scaling black-box solvers for discrete optimization. The method decomposes a large problem into fragments, repeatedly improves each fragment with the rest of the assignment held fixed, and then applies targeted corrections on unions of fragments. The solver itself is unchanged: it only receives a restricted subproblem and returns a candidate assignment. The framework separates decomposition from solver design. Moebius inversion gives an exact fragment expansion of the objective, and for pairwise objectives such as graph coloring, MAX-CUT, and QUBO the expansion closes at second order. The promoted solver is monotone by construction, terminates in finitely many productive sweeps for non-negative integer-valued objectives, and connects to junction-tree dynamic programming when the fragment interaction structure is acyclic and full response functions are propagated. On graph coloring benchmarks, the promoted versions of TabuSearch and simulated annealing (SA) generally outperform flat applications of the same solvers, often finding better solutions in less CPU time, and the gain proves insensitive to the choice of graph partition. A facility-location study delimits the claim: there the partition must respect the objective's interaction locality, and the promoted solver reaches within 0.3-1.4% of GLPK-certified optima at every tested size. The same wrapper interface is used in each solver-swap case, and the facility-location check reuses the same monotone guard with a sign-adjusted interaction diagnostic; the improvements therefore come from the MBE promotion mechanism rather than solver-specific tuning.

papers.title: A General Variable Neighborhood Search for Logistic Network Flow Design with Nonlinear Edge Costs and Transshipment Capacities
papers.abstract: We study the problem of routing multiple commodities through a logistic transport network so as to minimise the joint cost of vehicle movements and of transshipment (reload) operations at intermediate storages. The problem combines two features that are common in practice but rarely treated together: edge costs that are nonlinear in the transported volume, because freight is carried by vehicles of fixed capacity, and hard upper bounds on the volume that can be reloaded at each node. We formulate the problem as a mixed integer linear program in both an arc-based and a path-based form, derive its linear relaxation, and propose a metaheuristic solver based on General Variable Neighborhood Search (GVNS). The method works in the path space and relies on three problem-specific neighborhoods that generate new candidate paths by (i) shortest paths under a reload-aware metric, (ii) edges carrying partially loaded vehicles, and (iii) detours around congested storages. We evaluate the method on our open benchmark for this problem (arXiv:2606.20653): a corpus of realistic logistic networks calibrated on real road graphs of nine European countries, five U.S. states and the European part of Russia, with near-planar topology (Zipf city sizes, a spatial-network budget model, and a doubly constrained gravity demand model). On 35 synthetic and 15 real-geometry instances with up to 150 storages, GVNS returns solutions within about one percent of the best dual bound on small networks -- a branch-and-bound lower bound substantially tighter than the LP relaxation -- is stable across random seeds, and for a comparable wall-clock budget is up to 55% better than a time-limited exact solver on the medium instances.

papers.title: The SMFCE Paradigm: A Unified Modeling Framework Based on State, Cost, and Extremal Evolution
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a unified modeling framework centered on "state-cost-extremal evolution," referred to as the SMFCE paradigm. The paradigm represents the effective state of a system as a point in a state space, characterizes state cost by a single-valued scalar field, and describes system evolution through local cost descent or local extremum selection. Its mathematical core employs classical tools from differential geometry, gradient systems, and dynamical systems. The contribution of this paper is not to reintroduce these foundational results, but to organize them into two operational modeling principles. On finite-dimensional smooth Riemannian manifolds under appropriate regularity conditions, the path independence of cost differences and the cost monotonicity of negative gradient flows follow directly from classical results, while the descent property of discrete local-minimum transitions follows directly from the definition of a minimum. For same-level iterative emergence and present-centeredness, the paper provides conditional mathematical formulations using, respectively, parameterized gradient systems and bifurcation theory, and Markov processes and receding-horizon optimization. The paper further introduces three layered metrics: cost quantity, directed coupling degree, and commitment fulfillment rate, at the state, transition, path, and system levels. Finally, the paper discusses semantic modeling of large language model training and inference within this framework, explicitly distinguishes classical mathematical results, conditional propositions, and empirical adaptation models, and provides reproducible empirical testing procedures for the two modeling principles.

papers.title: The Last Iterate of the Projected Stochastic Subgradient Method Pays a Logarithm, Even in Dimension One
papers.abstract: We prove that the projected stochastic subgradient method with the standard anytime stepsizes $\eta_t = \gamma/\sqrt t$ can suffer expected last-iterate optimization error of order $(\log n)/\sqrt n$ already on the real line. Combined with the classical in-expectation upper bound, this establishes the sharp worst-case order of the projected stochastic subgradient method.

papers.title: Forward Tangent-Centered Sinkhorn DRO: Exact Nominal Recovery from Optimal Transport to KL
papers.abstract: Fixed-reference entropy-regularized transport yields smooth distributionally robust optimization (DRO) objectives, but its value as a function of the adversarial marginal is generally minimized at a kernel-smoothed law rather than at the nominal distribution. Consequently, the smallest raw ambiguity set need not recover nominal risk. Building on prior information-geometric plan-KL orientations, we study the forward tangent-centered discrepancy obtained by subtracting the value and first variation at the nominal law. This is the unique affine recentering, up to the simplex gauge; for symmetric costs, its plan-KL representation coincides with the forward candidate noted by Amari et al. (2018). The representation shows that the discrepancy dominates marginal KL, is uniquely zero at the nominal law, and is strongly convex in total variation. The resulting DRO problem retains a scalar log-sum-exp dual and closed-form conditional adversarial weights. On finite supports with symmetric zero-diagonal costs, the discrepancy converges uniformly to the unregularized transport cost at low temperature; for any finite cost, its rescaled value converges uniformly to marginal KL at high temperature. We derive its exact local Hessian, an explicit finite-sample containment radius, and a generalized chi-square calibration for multinomial data. Controlled simulations verify nominal centering, both limiting regimes, and practical plug-in coverage.

papers.title: Elimination Geometry II: Integrability, Representation, and Structural Limits
papers.abstract: Elimination geometry studies the exact nonnegative defect left after an auxiliary variable is optimized out. Part~II audits this certified-elimination interface through three theorem families. For integrability, local gaps form a repeated partial-elimination tower precisely under nonnegativity, touching, and zero elementary-square circulation. Hodge projection constructs nearest finite-space repairs and separates curvature, certification, and global period taxes. For representation and price, a descent gate characterizes surjective refinements and rules out strictly convex separable, duplication-invariant weight penalties. Dummy and target-calling lifts show that unrestricted lift design is vacuous, whereas the Fidelity-coherence frontier isolates irreducible cost. A modal Gram block classifies unconstrained quadratic lift-coupling germs and yields aligned Gaussian risk ledgers. Bernstein spectral functions preserve graph-Laplacian structure. Graph-universal Markov resolvents exist exactly up to first-order fractional qualification, and universal polynomial spectral penalties reduce to nonnegative Laplacian multiples. This linear limit does not preclude Part~I's nonlinear CDF repair and sharp CRPS theory. For converses, finite-order target-jet preservation uniquely requires subtraction of the corresponding defect jet, up to flat terms; approximate jets yield quasi-descent and stationary limits. Fixed-marginal coupling obeys a dependence-benefit frontier. Reversing certified KL in entropy-regularized control eliminates dimension-free guarantees, while a fixed measurement preserves all Umegaki defects of a faithful Gibbs family exactly when that family commutes.

papers.title: A reciprocal graph-deviation functional: structural identifiability from controlled equilibrium maps
papers.abstract: We constructed a reciprocal graph-deviation functional for positive ratios on a finite weighted graph. Its scalar generator $J(x)=\tfrac12(x+x^{-1})-1$ was characterized previously by ratio-composition and unit log-curvature. Our principal new result was structural identifiability: already on a two-site, one-edge system, the complete minimizer-location map obtained by sweeping the boundary and site-to-edge weight ratio determines any reciprocal generator whose log-coordinate representation is $C^2$ with everywhere-positive curvature, up to a positive scale; unit-curvature calibration fixes that scale. For the calibrated reciprocal family~$J_p$ we obtained the equilibrium response in closed form. A synthetic $15$-condition sweep with seven simulated measurements per condition and log-scale noise $\sigma=0.05$ selected $J$ over~$J_{1.1}$ with probability~$0.997$ under exact boundary and weight parameters; a declared representation-uncertainty screen lowered that value to approximately~$0.88$. These probabilities characterize the simulated design under the declared data-generating model. The finite sweep discriminated prespecified generators, whereas nonparametric recovery required the complete response map. We also recorded the associated convex gradient-flow and Langevin dynamics.
